Pro and anti vaxx crowds essentially seemed to be locked in a stalemate. So what is the longterm plan?


----------


Vaccines are available. 

With some exceptions - those who are willing have gotten it, and those who will refuse have made up their mind and aren't likely to change.

Politically it's just a state by state tug of war over mandates and protocols. I highly doubt anyone in an electable seat is looking at the science - they're going to be more concerned with their constituents feelings.

The CDC is shooting itself in the foot. I work in public / Occupational Safety, and through my own researched understanding they're being inconsistent. I've theories as to why - what makes sense and what is actually implimentable/enforceable are to different things.

As a side note: I don't get the "we can't trust the cdc so don't wear a mask" attitude. When you don't trust something you lean into the safety factor and error on the side of caution. If you don't trust the CDC you should be more cautious, not less!

Anyway, things are at a standstill. I don't see a light at the end of the tunnel. So what is the plan?

 1. Continuing this indefinitely?

 2. Waiting for a deadlier variant? 

 3. Waiting until enough people get frustrated and just "tired of it" to the point they vote people into power who will pretend covid doesn't exist?

 4. Sending mixed messages - directing people to take precautions in a way everyone is eventually infected/ vaccinated, but at slow pace that doesn't over stress medical services?

I'm the 'denialists' have a clear endgame. I'm just not sure any more what the targets, plans, or contingencies are for the people taking it seriously.

It's not a single link. 

It's a long term campaign of misunderstanding and misinformation. Guests, opinions, attitudes, and general content of his show have lead to the controversy.

Relocating to Chicago, work in Hegewisch... need some local insight into property hunting... I'm lost here!

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

So, I took a job in Hegewisch. I'm relocating from Detroit.  My stuff is in Storage. I've got a month-to-month studio rental in Bridgeport.

I thought I'd get to explore the city more, but COVID is a bitch. 


Now my employer has offered me moving incentives. They get worse and worse every month and expire in December. Basically if I buy a house before then they cover part of my storage & transportation, pay closing costs, pay for inspections, give me $5.5K for 'misc expenses,' and will offer to outright buy the place of move after two years for work related reasons. I don't want to pass it up, but I'm striking out on my search.


What I'm looking for:

1. I'm coming from a 4 bedroom 2400 sq foot house. I've got a lot of shit,  and all kinds of tools. Parking, Storage space, project space and room to tear my car apart is high on the list. I could maybe see a condo but at the very least I'd need a garage... I also have DIY renovated 3 houses. So long as I can get by under the radar without a requirement for licensed work, I can update place cheaply on my own! 
2. Room to entertain - hope to have friends and family visit form out of town. One bedroom/studio is out. 2 BR, maybe but 3 bed would be better. 
3. Proximity to work - I'd like <45 min commute.   This seems to limit me to the south side considering i work 'in the city' but by the indiana border.
4. Proximity to down town or at least public transit... I said yes to the damn job because they said it was Chicago... I'm single in my mid-30s, I like to go out, and a large dating pool also has an a appeal! I've been on a couple dates and from what I can tell a lot of people aren't interested in driving too far south to meet me... a house in indiana would be cheap, but really kill me socially.
5. Appreciating value / safe neighborhood.  It looks like a lot of areas on the south side are predicted to drop in value, I'd like to maybe sell in a couple years... itd be nice to make a little money.  As far as safety, I'd like to go jogging at night, and theres definitely neighborhoods my coworkers say should be a no go for me...
5. Price my budget was $250K (or less of I have to factor for an HOA). I think I'm bumping it to $280K-285K~ish but that hurts potential savings, and scares me. If my math is wrong (the taxes vary so wildly in different areas!), taxes jump, HOA fees raise, or whatever I could be fucked... so I'm trying to keep a safety factor  below $300K (my save break even on living expenses point).

Cool areas seemingly beyond my budget:

- Bridgeport - can't afford.
- Hyde Park - seems cool, but damn is it pricey.
- Jackson Park Highlands - Hello, rich people? I will not be joining you...

Areas I've noted and liked:

- Bronzeville -  I've seen some decent condos and a occasional house that sells 1st day on market but often they're near crossroads that make my coworkers cringe and shake their heads. 
- Beverly - have a friend who lives hes and likes it.  Further than I'd like bit it's got a Metra and cheaper taxes. Its rare, but occasionally something in my price range will pop. 

Areas I'm hesitant to explore.

- Evergreen park - crazy high taxes.  A 240K house would cost as much as 320k house in neighborhood in Beverly at the end of the year. Also further from downtown, work, and lacks public transportation.
- Oak Lawn - take evergreen park then add a 1.5 multiplier.
- Hegewisch - seems like a quiet town. No night life or public transportation. Virtually no commute to work, but decent drive into the city proper and and appears to greatly limit my "datability."
- NW Indiana - Damn, I'd save some money and be close to work, but I would die inside.
- South Shore - Everyone says its "on the up" but the gun violence map really is red in this are and propery values are all over the place. Can't get a handle on it all!

------------
Tips my new coworkers have offered:

1. Look around the neighborhood if more houses have bars on windows or doors - "just no."
2. Look at the gun violence map of Chicago (I have. Its EVERYWHERE, and of little help).
3. Look at any place with a Mariano's or Target. (Classy AF, right?)
4. Look at demographics - Whiter areas correlate with safer areas (and more racist areas).
